Overview

Why Modularity and Interoperability?

Scaling in-space missions into commercial services will require a new generation of autonomous robots capable of operating across diverse platforms, missions, and service providers. Achieving this vision depends on embedding modularity and interoperability into the design, development, and operation of space robots and supporting infrastructure.

While significant advances have been made in robotic manipulation, autonomous operations, and servicing technologies, the absence of common interfaces, standards, and interoperable architectures remains a major barrier to scalability and commercial adoption.

This workshop will identify key technical, operational, and regulatory challenges and explore opportunities for standardization and cross-sector collaboration — with a focus on how modular and interoperable robotic ecosystems can reduce costs, increase flexibility, enable sustainable space operations, and unlock a thriving in-space economy.

Index Terms — Autonomous systems, interoperability, in-orbit services, modularity, space robotics

Visual Inspirations

Modular & Interoperable Space Robotics

From reconfigurable manipulators and modular orbital platforms to interoperable lunar mobility concepts, these conceptual examples from the literature reflect the type of robotic ecosystems the workshop aims to enable: adaptable, serviceable, and scalable across missions and environments.

Reconfigurable Walking Manipulators
A representative vision of orbital systems assembled from interoperable modules, supporting inspection, servicing, assembly, and long-term reconfiguration.
Source: Space Applications Services — Walking Manipulator ↗
Orbital Infrastructure Assembly with Modular Mobile Robotics
A conceptual vision of modular mobile robots assembling and traversing large orbital structures, illustrating how reconfigurable robotic systems and standardized interfaces can support scalable in-space infrastructure construction.
Source: Acta Astronautica (2025) ↗
Interoperable Surface Robotics
Modular rover concepts illustrate how interoperable subsystems can support resilient, mission-flexible operations for planetary exploration and logistics.
Source: Post et al., Acta Astronautica (2021) ↗

Panel Discussion

The town-hall panel will bring together expert panelists and the audience to explore technical, operational, commercial, and policy challenges. Particular attention will be given to common interfaces, standards, certification approaches, business incentives, and the collaborative frameworks required to transition from proprietary solutions towards open, scalable ecosystems.

Workshop Chairs

Organizers

Prof (Hon.) Dr Mini C. Rai

Founder & Director
Orbit Rise Ltd, UK
With over 30 years of experience in space engineering and robotics, Mini has led numerous national and international programmes in orbital and planetary robotics. She is a co-author of the 2025 Position Paper on Robot Modularity, Interoperability and Standards published by the UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency.
dr_minicrai@orbitrise.co.uk

Dr Marco De Stefano

Head — Floating-base Robot Control Group
Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics, German Aerospace Center (DLR), Germany
Marco holds a master's in Astronautical Engineering (Sapienza) and a PhD in Mechatronics (UNIMORE). His PhD thesis was a finalist for the 2020 Georges Giralt Award and he was a finalist for the 2023 KUKA Innovation Award. He currently serves as Project Manager for the ESA RISE mission development at German Aerospace Center (DLR).
marco.destefano@dlr.de

Dr Manu H. Nair

Lecturer (Asst. Prof) in Space Engineering
University of Manchester, UK
Manu received his PhD in space robotics from the University of Lincoln, where he developed the End-Over-End Walking Manipulator for future ISAM operations. His research focuses on robotics in extreme environments and advanced space systems engineering.
manu.nair@manchester.ac.uk

Early Career Researchers

Call for Poster Presentations

Early-career researchers, industrialists, and academics are invited to present their latest work through poster presentations. Selection will prioritise direct relevance to the workshop topic, with equity, diversity, and inclusion also considered. Posters will be evaluated by a multidisciplinary panel from industry, academia, and space agencies.

Poster abstract submission deadline is 16 October 2026.

All selected poster presenters must register for the conference using the registration link. Registration opens on 31 August 2026, and closes on 23 October 2026. Early-bird rates available until 24 September 2026.

After the Workshop

A workshop outcomes report capturing key discussions, findings, and recommendations will be published.
